title: How Species Are Named
hook: Every species on Earth gets a two-word Latin name — like Homo sapiens — under a tidy ranked system invented 250 years ago that scientists still use today.
key_points: Linnaean classification nests life in ranks: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
Each species gets a two-part scientific name: its genus plus a species label.
This binomial naming is written in italics, genus capitalized — e.g. Homo sapiens.
Carl Linnaeus formalized the system in the 1700s, giving every species one universal name.
Universal names avoid confusion from local common names that vary by language and place.
content_html: Biologists organize life with a system of nested ranks: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species, each narrower than the last. At the finest level, every species earns a unique two-word name — its genus followed by a species label. Humans are Homo sapiens; the genus is capitalized and the whole thing is italicized. This is called binomial nomenclature, and it gives scientists everywhere a shared, unambiguous label for each kind of organism.
extra_html: The framework comes from the 18th-century Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus, who set out to give every living thing one consistent name and a fixed place in a hierarchy. His big idea was the two-part name: rather than long descriptive phrases or local nicknames, each species got a compact genus-plus-species tag. That matters because common names are a mess — a single bird might be called different things in every town and language, while Turdus migratorius means exactly one thing to a biologist in any country. As Encyclopaedia Britannica describes, modern taxonomy still rests on this Linnaean skeleton, even as DNA reshuffles which organisms belong where.

related.title: The Kingdoms of Life
related.hook: One step below the domains, life sorts into kingdoms — animals, plants, fungi, and assorted microbes — each a different way of making a living on Earth.

related.title: The Three Domains of Life
related.hook: At the very top, all life splits into just three branches — Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya — and your cells belong to the same one as mushrooms and oak trees.

related.title: A Hidden Bird Species, Revealed by DNA
related.hook: Two birds in Japan look nearly identical — but their DNA and songs say they're different species. The split is Japan's first new bird in 40 years, and shows how genetics keeps finding hidden life.

flashcards.back_html: A two-part name made of an organism's genus plus its species label — for example, Homo sapiens for humans. The genus is capitalized and both are italicized.

flashcards.prompt: Who formalized the system of ranking and naming species we still use?
flashcards.explanation_html: Carl Linnaeus laid out the nested ranks and two-word naming in the 1700s. Darwin and Mendel came later and worked on evolution and heredity, not the naming system.

flashcards.prompt: Why do scientists use Latin binomial names instead of common names?

choices.text: Common names vary by language and region, while one binomial is universal
Latin names are shorter than common names
Common names are illegal in science

flashcards.explanation_html: A single creature might have dozens of common names across languages, but one binomial name is recognized worldwide, removing ambiguity.
